# R270 — CPU pool scheduling and segmented verifier decode critical path

Date: 2026-10-12 (JST). Read-only source audit of integrated WN `sync-xe-v0143-nonfinite-20261012`, HEAD `0691bcdf5af63a85b3b25650f367d3276db64035`, plus registry v162 and primary-source scheduling references. No project-source edit, build, test, profiler, AST/lint, CPU/GPU/model run, Git operation, cleanup, process query, or active Main-log read. Main is independently collecting `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING`; this review did not inspect that run. The user's Ryzen 5600X / Arc B570 10 GiB, H=2560, FF=640, K=10, 262,144 max context, 32K decode mean 7.86 tok/s, and one-thread synthetic GU/Down intervals 0.14–0.32 / 0.036–0.097 ms are supplied context only. The synthetic intervals do not identify model decode's critical path.

## Finding

The current source can discriminate broad host/dispatch/verification spans, route counts, and host wall time for the native CPU pool's GU, serial intermediate quantization, and Down phases. It cannot establish exclusive CPU busy time, worker imbalance, worker cache-miss behavior, or an additive CPU-versus-GPU critical-path equation. In segmented verifier mode, the CPU services the layer/group after the GPU has reached its expert boundary; queued expert copies are drained and checked before the next graph segment launches. That path has a real serial host-service boundary, but existing totals cannot tell how much of it is native row computation versus dispatch, barriers, or PCIe/copy handling.

R267's v158 arm labels are corrected by registry v162: they were **nonfinite / `NAN_GUARD` ON/OFF**, not overlap ON/OFF. They cover 32,768 input IDs, not a 262,144-position full-context run. Their endpoint values remain as recorded, but they provide no overlap or critical-path evidence. Likewise, the supplied 7.86 tok/s average and synthetic one-thread timings do not determine whether changing the pool helps.

## What the existing counters mean

`STRATA_DECODE_TIMING` snapshots verifier and dispatch counters at request start/end and emits `strata decode timing:` per request. It reports windows, mean T/tokens per window and physical decode/window time, then `verify` elapsed split as GPU-reach wait, per-layer host (`plan`, input activation quantize, jobs, CPU callback) and stage; commit/emit, draft, per-layer-window CPU expert/miss/VRAM-hit/PCIe counts; before-window and adaptive join/adapt time. These fields identify whether attention should move to verifier reach, host callback/dispatch, commit/draft, or routing. They are nested or overlapping host intervals; adding them does not recover wall time or exclusive CPU work. The printed PCIe value is a count of distinct experts per layer-window, not bytes or H2D duration.

The source also accumulates `ExpertPool::ms_multi_gu`, `ms_multi_q`, and `ms_multi_down`. `run_split_multi_native` times GU-row pool phases, the serial caller-thread quantization between phases, then Down-row pool phases. The summary prints these as `pool multi` milliseconds per decode round, plus `pool.multi_bytes / (GU + Down)` as a logical submitted-blob-bytes rate and CPU-pool-call elapsed time. These are not worker CPU-time totals. GU/Down include barrier/scheduling/claim/wait costs; GU and Down can overlap GPU work in paths that permit it. The byte rate counts logical blob extent submitted, not DRAM transactions or bytes measured at the memory controller.

Crucially, `STRATA_DECODE_TIMING` does not snapshot or print the three `ms_multi_*` phase counters. The later `pool multi` line divides pool-lifetime accumulated counters by decode `rounds`, not request-local deltas. `Prefill` can use this same pool when `STRATA_PREFILL_CPU_SHARE` is nonzero/auto, the prompt chunk is below `STREAM_ALL_MIN` (2,048), and the backend reports concurrent host handoff; those prompt calls can enter the same native multi-token timers. The pool byte counter is also cumulative. Thus the line is a useful coarse phase clue only after confirming no earlier work contributed (or after a request-local counter baseline is available); do not treat it as a clean per-request decode measurement by default.

In `Verifier::run`'s segmented route, for each layer/group it waits for the GPU graph segment to complete and verifies the host doorbell sequence before calling the host/pool callback. The callback makes its pool plan and runs CPU jobs; the verifier then `stream_sync(copy_)` checks copy completion and errors before it publishes host flags and launches the next segment. This is the required ownership boundary: the GPU-visible host data/copy staging must not be read or reused before its completion event/stream completion. The source's checked `stream_sync` and `dma_error_` path remains mandatory. `ver.ms_wait` is the elapsed time from entering the GPU-boundary wait through ring completion; `ver.ms_pool` includes work after that boundary through CPU callback, copy drain, flag/service and next-segment submission. `drive.d.ms_run` is a nested host dispatch callback span, not an independent addend. These spans can show where elapsed time accumulates, but cannot isolate which CPU worker or exact instruction stalls it.

## Current CPU task and placement policy

`ExpertPool` uses one thread per allowed physical core, selected by package/core sysfs identity with one logical CPU per core; `physical_cores(true)` removes the first core from the worker list. `SessionLoopScratch::init` pins the decode caller/host thread to the first allowed physical core for its lifetime and restores affinity on teardown. On the supplied 6C/12T machine, the default is therefore five pinned worker threads plus the pinned caller participating as the sixth CPU worker (`--no-host-worker` disables the caller's work). The startup log reports task count and participating threads. Explicit `--pool-workers N` fixes worker count; values above five on this six-core host would create at least one unpinned worker, so the bounded first sweep should stay at 3–5 workers. The normal source path avoids placing one worker on each SMT sibling; do not infer that 12 logical threads are the right default.

For segmented native verify, CPU jobs are grouped by distinct expert IDs for a window. `run_split_multi_native` flattens each batch's expert-row ranges: GU has `n_experts × FF` rows and Down has `n_experts × H`; each phase divides its total rows into equal contiguous task ranges. `--pool-tasks 0` uses three tasks per participating thread, capped by phase row count. A positive `--pool-tasks N` sets `min(rows, N)` tasks per phase. The shared epoch/head counter hands these equal row chunks dynamically to whichever worker claims next; there is no fixed expert-to-core partition. Each worker owns private scratch; job activation and output tables are shared. For a fixed expert count, fewer tasks mean larger contiguous row chunks and less scheduler traffic but potentially a longer tail. More tasks improve redistribution opportunities while increasing epoch/head claims and potentially splitting one expert's contiguous weight rows across workers. These are candidates to measure, not predictions.

No project source field or CLI setting assigns expert jobs to a specific CPU cache domain; the scheduler is work-stealing across the pinned physical-core set. The 5600X is a single-socket consumer CPU, so a NUMA shard strategy has no source-grounded role here. Keep the packed expert source/mmap/resident tier, worker affinity, caller-core affinity, data residency, and 262,144 max-context setting fixed during the first task/thread sweep. Any memory/cache hierarchy claim requires target-specific measurement; Intel's general advice is to balance work while minimizing data movement and verify the running application.

## Existing safe CPU/PCIe work distribution

This WN has **no `STRATA_PCIE_*` environment knob** in the searched engine source. The active setting is `--pcie-frac` (plus `--pcie-mode`), with model defaults/probe when no explicit fraction is supplied. A native pack begins with its default fraction (0.55) adjusted by the startup host-to-device bandwidth probe; the canonical pack default is 0.2. `setup_pcie_split` can additionally measure representative CPU expert time, GPU expert time, PCIe fetch time, and shared-memory slowdown, then use `pcie_split_m` to evaluate how many distinct missed experts should be sent to the GPU. It tests candidate splits and retains a nonzero split only when modeled completion time is at least 10% below all-CPU service. In the per-window dispatcher, the calibrated split is gated on a device-readable alias for the source; otherwise the GPU gets no PCIe-shared misses and the CPU keeps them. With a usable source alias, it sends only the last `m` distinct misses in the routing order (resident experts and helper-held experts are already excluded). When an explicit `--pcie-frac` is supplied, setup retains that setting instead of deriving the measured split; do not describe explicit share selection as the measured optimizer.

Segmented verifier code drains the copy stream and checks `dma_error_`/the expected publication flag before starting the next segment. Keep this completion ordering, any staging-source lifetime, and existing host/device publication unchanged. During a CPU-pool tuning comparison, hold the exact `pcie_frac` and `pcie_mode` behavior constant, record their effective startup values, and retain the same resident/cache profile. Do not hand-assign more misses to PCIe based on the synthetic CPU numbers or on 32K counters mislabeled as overlap.

## Bounded next action after the current baseline closes

1. Preserve the Main-owned baseline and its output/status evidence. For each completed fresh 32K sample, pair the `strata decode timing:` request line with that request's `pool multi`, decode summary, exact `max_context=262144`, actual input-position count, model/cache/profile, MTP/window distribution, worker/task startup line, `pcie_frac`/mode and effective environment. Do not read the live Main log while it is active. The timing line's `CPU`/per-layer host and verifier reach/host/stage spans provide the request-level discriminator; inspect whether the pool summary is decode-only by checking Prefill CPU-share/chunk conditions or, if not, label it cumulative.
2. If host-side CPU dispatch and the segmented post-ring service are exposed on physical window wall, first screen fixed worker counts `--pool-workers 3, 4, 5` with `--pool-tasks 0` (automatic), no other changes. This tests capacity/affinity while retaining dynamic task assignment. Keep `--no-host-worker` as a separate, explicitly paired arm only if host-core interference is the question; it changes both the pool's participant count and automatic task count.
3. At the best fixed worker count, compare task counts `6, 12, 18, 24` against auto (`0`); row counts cap the realized tasks. The automatic baseline on default five workers + caller is 18 tasks per eligible phase. Keep routing, PCIe fraction/mode, prefill chunk/share, cache profile, context, MTP and output/correctness gates fixed. Capture all startup/route/decode summaries; if the small sample does not show a consistent wall-time change, stop before implementation work.
4. Treat the given one-thread synthetic GU/Down numbers only as a comparison baseline for the same synthetic harness. They can help verify kernel scaling under controlled memory/data placement; they cannot replace paired model decode timing. Do not use profiler, per-thread tracing, additional tests/builds, or full-context input until separately authorized. Preserve `max_context=262144`; a 32K prompt remains a 32K actual input, not a full-context validation.

For each arm, compare paired independent-process fresh-first decode wall/tok/s and successful outputs, retain failures, and report the distribution rather than the best run. A timing win is only attributable to pool thread/task scheduling if all other route and state inputs match. The next precise unresolved question after these existing timers is worker imbalance versus kernel service versus task-claim/barrier cost; only then would a narrowly scoped worker-claim/worker-active measurement be justified.

## External primary evidence

Intel's VTune tuning recipe explains the relevant general tradeoff: dynamic assignment can reduce imbalance, while fine chunks add scheduling overhead; it recommends detecting which applies before changing grain. Its worked sample is OpenMP on a Xeon Gold, not Strata's C++ pool on Ryzen, so it informs a bounded A/B and not an expected gain. [Intel VTune: OpenMP imbalance and scheduling overhead](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/docs/vtune-profiler/cookbook/2024-1/openmp-imbalance-and-scheduling-overhead.html). Intel's NUMA guidance likewise says place work and data near consuming cores and measure the real application; it does not imply a NUMA optimization on this supplied desktop [Intel: hardware/software approach for NUMA systems](https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/developer/articles/technical/hardware-and-software-approach-for-using-numa-systems.html).

As a code comparator, current llama.cpp ggml CPU threadpool uses a shared atomic `current_chunk` to distribute work chunks, and its MoE RFC describes cache placement/split ideas with separate graph-input and mapping constraints. This supports the category of comparing chunk granularity and cache strategy, not copying its execution policy or benchmark results: different kernels, model quantization, hardware, route, and runtime. [ggml CPU threadpool source](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ggml-cpu.c), [llama.cpp CPU MoE cache RFC](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/28248).

This is a static assessment. No critical-path conclusion can be made until Main's baseline closes and exact request-level timing/route evidence is reviewed under the stated restrictions. No candidate or expected speedup is asserted.
